summary.title: 6 Techniques I Use to Create a Great User Experience for Shell Scripts
summary.one_liner: Six shell-scripting techniques for friendly, safe, and informative scripts, illustrated with the evaluation script the author wrote for the One Billion Row Challenge.
takeaways: Print clear usage and error messages and validate arguments up front, e.g. checking whether $1 is empty.
Use ANSI color codes such as bold red for errors and send messages to stderr.
Wrap commands in a helper function that echoes each command before running it, similar to bash set -x.
Use set -e and set +e strategically so one failing sub-task does not abort the whole run, while script bugs still exit.
Detect the OS with uname and fall back to alternatives such as gtimeout on macOS; timestamp output files so repeated runs do not overwrite results.
summary.summary: The author describes six techniques used in a Bash evaluation script written for the One Billion Row Challenge: input validation with usage messages, colored ANSI output, a print_and_execute wrapper that logs commands, selective use of set -e and set +e, OS-specific handling (Linux vs macOS gtimeout), and timestamped output files. Each technique is shown with a short code snippet from the script. The post is a practical, example-driven tutorial aimed at making scripts easier and safer to use.
